name: Dropped third strike, bases loaded, 2 outs
offense: The batter can run because there are two outs, even though first base is occupied. Everyone runs: every runner is forced to move up. Batter: drop the bat and sprint to first right away.
defense: Every base is a force. The simplest out is often for the catcher to pick up the ball and step on home plate, or throw to first. Don't rush into a wild throw: one clean force ends the inning.
common_mistakes: Batter walks back to the dugout thinking it's over; runners stop; catcher tags the batter late or throws wildly instead of taking the sure force at home.

name: Dropped third strike, runner on first, 1 out
offense: With first base occupied and fewer than two outs, the batter is out and can't run, whether or not the catcher holds the pitch. The runner on first is NOT forced; he may try to advance at his own risk.
defense: The batter is already out. Don't throw to first; watch the runner. Keep the ball in front, call 'batter's out' loudly so the infield knows, and only throw if the runner is trying to advance.
common_mistakes: Defense throws to first for a batter who is already out and lets the runner take extra bases; batter runs when he can't and draws a throw that helps no one.

name: Dropped third strike, runner on third, 1 out
offense: First base is open, so the batter can run: sprint to first the moment the ball gets away. The runner on third watches the catcher: if the catcher throws to first, that's often the chance to break for home.
defense: Tag the batter if he's close, or throw to first. Before throwing, check the runner on third; the corner infielders should call it out. A rushed throw can give away the winning run.
common_mistakes: Batter doesn't run because he thinks strike three ends it; runner on third doesn't read the throw; catcher throws to first without looking the runner back.

name: Runner hit by a fair batted ball, bases loaded, no outs
offense: One out, and the inning isn't over. A runner hit by a fair batted ball that no fielder has touched is out, and the ball is dead at that moment, even if it later rolls foul. Nothing after the dead ball counts. The batter is awarded first base and only forced runners move up one base, so with the bases loaded: the batter goes to first, the runner from first to second, the runner from second to third, and no run scores. Coaches: when you hear 'dead ball', stop calling for runners to go and let the umpires place them.
defense: Once the umpire calls dead ball, tags and throws don't count, however good they were: hold the ball and let the umpires place the runners. The key judgment is whether a fielder touched the ball before it hit the runner. If she did, the ball stays live and the runner isn't out unless she interfered on purpose, so the tags that followed would count.
common_mistakes: The umpire calls the runner out but doesn't kill the play loudly, so everyone keeps playing; a second umpire calls more outs on a ball that was already dead; coaches yell players into extra running and tagging; the crew changes a call because of the noise instead of getting together. Fix: 'Time! Dead ball!' with both arms up, a quick crew conference, then one calm explanation to each coach.

name: Slow roller rolls foul, then back fair before first base
offense: It's a fair ball, so the batter is a runner and the out at first stands. A ground ball that hasn't reached first or third base isn't foul just because it crossed the line: it's judged where it stops or where a fielder first touches it. This one rolled foul, came back, and was picked up in fair territory, so it was fair and in play. Umpires usually signal a fair ball by pointing toward fair territory without saying anything; only foul is called out loud. Batter: run on every ball you hit until you hear 'Foul!' or 'Time!'
defense: Pick the ball up and make the play: step on first or throw there. A slow roller near the line that's still rolling can be left alone; if it stops or you touch it in foul territory before it reaches the base, it's foul. Fielders, like batters, play until the umpire stops it.
common_mistakes: The batter stands at the plate because the ball crossed the line once; the fielder picks it up and freezes; the umpire's fair signal is late or small, so nobody sees it; coaches on both sides shout directions and the players try to learn the rule in the middle of the play. Fix: the plate umpire points fair clearly the moment the ball is touched in fair territory, and coaches teach 'run until you hear foul' at practice, not during the play.
verify_note: Our wording of the general fair/foul rule for a ground ball before first or third base (baseball and softball). No rulebook definition text is loaded yet (see gaps.csv). Fair or foul is the umpire's judgment and can't be protested (F015, F087, F199, F032). Scenario from Sean (2026-10-23).

name: Two runners on the same base
offense: Both runners stay on the base until the umpire rules; never step off thinking you're out. The base belongs to the lead runner unless the lead runner was forced to advance; then it belongs to the trailing runner. The runner who isn't entitled to the base looks to the coach: go back to the base they came from if it's open and they can make it.
defense: Tag both runners while they're on the base. The umpire calls out the one who wasn't entitled to it, so tagging both removes the guesswork. Then look for the next play.
common_mistakes: A runner walks off the base thinking the play is over and gets tagged; the fielder tags only one runner, the wrong one; the trailing runner freezes between bases instead of checking the coach.

name: Fly ball with fewer than two outs
offense: On a deep fly ball, go back and tag up: leave only after the catch, on the coach's call. On a shallow fly, go halfway, or as far as you can and still get back, so you can advance if it drops or return if it's caught. Never run on contact with fewer than two outs on a ball in the air.
defense: Catch it, then throw ahead of the lead runner to the base they're heading for, through the cut-off. If a runner left before the catch, appeal by throwing to that base before the runner gets back.
common_mistakes: Running on contact with fewer than two outs and getting doubled off; leaving the base before the catch; tagging up on a shallow fly and getting thrown out.

name: Two outs: run on contact
offense: With two outs, every runner runs on any batted ball. If the ball is caught the inning is over anyway, so there's nothing to protect; if it drops or gets through, runs score. Run hard and find the base coach.
defense: Take the sure out. With two outs, get the force at the closest base or the out at first; don't chase the lead runner.
common_mistakes: Runners waiting on a fly ball with two outs; fielders trying for a harder play instead of the easy force that ends the inning.

name: Runner on second, ground ball, fewer than two outs
offense: Ball hit in front of you (to the shortstop or third baseman): hold, unless you're forced. Ball hit behind you (to the right side): go to third. If first base is also occupied you're forced, so run. Line drive: freeze until it goes through.
defense: Look the runner back before throwing to first. If the runner breaks for third on a ball hit in front of them, throw to third.
common_mistakes: Running into an out on a ball hit to the left side; forgetting you're forced when first base is occupied; breaking on a line drive and getting doubled off.

name: Rounding a base: find the base coach
offense: Pick up the base coach before you reach the base. Round it hard only when the coach waves you on; stop and get back on a stop sign. When the ball is behind you, the coach makes the call; at third base the third-base coach decides whether you score.
defense: Throw behind a runner who rounds too far, and hit the cut-off so trailing runners can't take an extra base.
common_mistakes: Running with your head down and missing the stop sign; watching the ball instead of the coach when it's behind you; slowing down before the coach gives a sign.
